forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: North West Leicestershire flags housing account sustainability risk as reserves fall
news_drafts.lead: North West Leicestershire's housing account faces sustainability risks as unrestricted reserves—money the council can actually spend—fall to critical levels, the council warned this week. Reserves stand at £1.688m, only 68% above the statutory minimum of £1.000m. Consecutive years of financial pressure have driven this decline, with operating expenditure, the cost of day-to-day running, exceeding forecast by £0.293m in the first quarter of 2026/27 alone. Maintenance costs are running £1.022m over budget due to increased repairs activity and £0.204m in compensation for historic repair failures. The council has cut planned debt repayment by 27%, from £1.319m to £1.000m, to manage the pressure, while allocating £0.735m to building reserves.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget Setting 2027/28 - Update one Cabinet Report
findings.headline: Council tax support claimants stand at 4,662 (1,964 pensioners and 2,698 working age), against 4,652 in the previous financial year.
findings.detail: The paper describes the caseload as relatively stable over the previous three years. It notes that any increase in support cases reduces the tax base and adds pressure to balancing the budget.
findings.matters: Growth in support cases lowers collectable council tax, so a finance director would track this figure alongside the tax base.
findings.figures: 4,662 claimants (currently); 1,964 pensioners; 2,698 working age; 4,652 (previous financial year)
findings.quote: There are currently 4662 (1964 pensioners and 2698 working age) council tax support claimants.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget Setting 2027/28 - Update one Cabinet Report
findings.headline: The pause in Local Government Reorganisation was announced on 7 September 2026, and the timetable for unpausing is not yet known.
findings.detail: The paper says the MTFP was prepared on the basis of Local Government Reorganisation, and officers will keep working on a plan that assumes the council continues for the life of the MTFP. The 2028/29 budget was to be the first year of the new Leicestershire and Rutland council.
findings.matters: A pause in a reorganisation that was meant to start in 2028/29 changes the budget horizon for any council in the county and affects Section 24 controls.
findings.figures: 7 September 2026 (pause announced); 2028/29 (expected first year of the new council)
findings.quote: up until 7 September when the pause was announced

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget Setting 2027/28 - Update one Cabinet Report
findings.headline: The reset of the business rates system from April 2026 has meant a considerable reduction in retained business rates.
findings.detail: The paper says transitional funding in the 2026/27 settlement protected the council from a cliff-edge drop. It says the reset has reduced retained rates and that growth projected since then is unlikely to return income to pre-reset levels. Business rates growth had previously funded the capital programme.
findings.matters: The business rates reset is a structural change in how councils fund themselves, and a council that previously used rate growth for capital will have less room to do the same.
findings.quote: there will be a considerable reduction in retained business rates.

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget Setting 2027/28 - Update one Cabinet Report
findings.headline: The council tax base was 39,152 at 9 October 2026, against a budgeted base of 38,909 before the 2.5% non-collection allowance.
findings.detail: The paper says the tax base has achieved the budgeted base. It notes continuing uncertainty about collectability, support cases and future growth. Over the period since 2022/23 the base grew by 3,328 Band D equivalents, or 9.4% cumulatively.
findings.matters: A tax base ahead of budget supports council tax income assumptions, and the paper's uncertainty comments show what a finance director would test next.
findings.figures: 39,152 (council tax base at 9 October 2026); 38,173 after 2.5% non-collection allowance; 38,909 budgeted base; 37,927 budgeted base after allowance; 3,328 increase since 2022/23; 9.4% cumulative growth; 2.25% average annual growth
findings.quote: As of 9 October 2026, the Council tax-base is 39,152 (38,173 taking into account the 2.5% non collection allowance)

findings.paper_title: General Fund Budget Setting 2027/28 - Update one Cabinet Report
findings.headline: The Fair Funding grant in the assumed grant table falls from £19.1m in 2026/27 to £13.7m in 2027/28 and £8m in each of 2028/29 and 2029/30.
findings.detail: The grants table is for the 2026-2029 spending review period. The paper states that no announcement has yet been made that this funding will continue beyond that period, and that extending the grants would significantly reduce the 2029/30 savings required.
findings.matters: Fair Funding is the largest grant line in the table, so its decline is the main driver of the medium-term gap, and other councils' grant assumptions will face the same question.
findings.quote: At the point of publication, there has been no announcement that this funding will continue into future years.
